Distribution Function of the Modified Half-Normal Distribution

Source: R/pmhn.R
pmhn.Rd

Computes the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the Modified Half-Normal (MHN) distribution with parameters alpha, beta, and gamma.

Usage

pmhn(q, alpha = 1, beta = 1, gamma = 0, lower.tail = TRUE, log.p = FALSE)

Arguments

q

Numeric vector of quantiles.

alpha

Shape parameter (\(\alpha > 0\)). Scalar or numeric vector. Default: 1.

beta

Rate-type parameter (\(\beta > 0\)), the coefficient of the Gaussian tail \(\exp(-\beta x^2)\); larger values pull mass toward zero. Scalar or numeric vector. Default: 1.

gamma

Tilt parameter (\(\gamma \in R\)), the coefficient of the exponential tilt \(\exp(\gamma x)\). Scalar or numeric vector. Default: 0.

lower.tail

Logical; if TRUE (default), probabilities are \(P(X \le q)\), otherwise \(P(X > q)\).

log.p

Logical; if TRUE, probabilities are returned on the log scale. Default: FALSE. Both flags are read with as.logical(), so that 1 is TRUE; a value that gives NA is an error.

Value

A numeric vector. The output length equals max(length(q), length(alpha), length(beta), length(gamma)), or 0 if any of them has length zero; each input is recycled to that length following standard R recycling rules. For q <= 0 the CDF is 0; for q = Inf it is 1. As in pgamma, an element whose parameters lie outside the parameter space (alpha or beta not positive and finite, or gamma not finite) is NaN, with a warning, and an element with an NA or NaN among its inputs is NA or NaN (NA if any of them is NA), without one; the other elements are unaffected. The arguments must be numeric (double, integer or logical): a factor, a character string, a complex number, a list or NULL is an error, as in pnorm. As with pnorm, the attributes of q (names, dim, dimnames) are kept when the result has the length of q; a classed q, such as a Date, is taken as its numbers and gives a plain vector. Unlike pnorm, attributes of a longer parameter vector are not carried over.

Details

In the general case the lower tail is computed, where that is accurate (see below), from the series representation (Sun et al. 2023, Lemma 1b) $$F(x \mid \alpha, \beta, \gamma) = \frac{1}{\Psi[\alpha/2, \gamma/\sqrt{\beta}]} \sum_{i=0}^{\infty} \frac{z^i}{i!}\, \Gamma(s_i)\, P(s_i, \beta x^2)$$ where \(z = \gamma/\sqrt{\beta}\), \(s_i = (\alpha + i)/2\), and \(P(s, y)\) is the regularized lower incomplete gamma function.

The default parameters alpha = 1, beta = 1, gamma = 0 correspond to the half-normal distribution \(\mathrm{HN}(1/\sqrt{2})\).

At \(\gamma = 0\) and at \(\alpha = 1\) exactly the distribution function is computed from the law it reduces to; a shape or a tilt merely close to those values is a different law, and is computed as in the general case:

  • \(\gamma = 0\): \(F(q) = P(\alpha/2, \beta q^2)\), the regularized incomplete gamma function of the square-root-Gamma law (Sun et al. 2023, Lemma 6a), for \(\alpha \le 10^6\); a larger shape is computed as in the general case.

  • \(\alpha = 1\): the truncated-normal CDF (Sun et al. 2023, Lemma 6b). Near the truncation point the lower tail keeps its relative accuracy however small it is. Where \(-\gamma/\sqrt{2\beta}\) overflows the law is Exponential with rate \(|\gamma|\).

The series is used, where it is accurate, for \(\alpha \le 100\) with \(|z| \le 20\), and for \(\alpha < 1\) up to \(|z|\) of about 830 (for \(|z| > 20\) it costs milliseconds per value); elsewhere the lower tail is computed by numerical integration of the density. The upper tail \(P(X > q)\) is computed directly, by numerical integration of the density over \((q, \infty)\), and not as \(1 - F\), which would round to 0 once it falls below about \(10^{-16}\). Each tail is computed directly on its own side of the peak of the density of \(\log X\), which lies at or above the median, and as one minus the other tail beyond it. For a large shape or tilt, where the terms of these forms grow too large, both tails are measured from that peak instead. With log.p = TRUE both tails are formed on the log scale throughout, so that \(\log F\) is still resolved where \(F\) rounds to 1 or is below the smallest positive double, and a log probability close to 0, about minus the other tail, keeps the relative accuracy of that other tail to within about \(10^{-9}\) (Appendix A.4 of the vignette cited below).

Accuracy and range. With \(z = \gamma/\sqrt{\beta}\) as above, for \(\alpha \le 10^{15}\), \(|z| \le 10^{15}\) and \(\beta\) in \([10^{-300}, 10^{300}]\) both tails are accurate to the working tolerance sqrt(.Machine$double.eps) within 10 standard deviations of the peak, and to about twice that beyond. Outside that range the law can be narrower than the spacing of the doubles near its peak (for \(z\) above about \(10^{16}\), or \(\alpha\) above about \(10^{31}\)); the probabilities are then still those of the exact law at the doubles q given, a step from 0 to 1 between two adjacent doubles, whose value at the double nearest the peak is set by where the peak lies within its spacing. Two cases give NA with a warning instead: within 45 standard deviations of the peak of a law whose peak cannot be placed to within \(10^{-11}\) of its standard deviation, which needs a law narrower than the spacing by a factor of order \(10^{19}\) or more and then happens for some parameters only (as at \(\alpha = \beta = \gamma = 10^{200}\)); and where the whole law lies beyond the largest double without a positive tilt to place it (a shape near the largest double against a subnormal \(\beta\)). A third case lies at the other end of the range: where \(\beta\) and the tilt are both close to the largest double (\(\beta\) from about \(2 \times 10^{307}\) with \(\gamma\) near the largest double, or from about \(5 \times 10^{307}\) with \(\gamma\) from about \(10^{306}\)), at some points \(q\) above the peak where \(\beta q\) is above about half the largest double, the log upper tail is -Inf where it is finite (the upper tail itself is then 0, which is its value in double precision), and next to the point where \(\beta q\) overflows both are NA with a warning. Where \(z\) itself overflows, the law is its limit: Gamma(\(\alpha\), rate \(|\gamma|\)) under a negative tilt, and normal about its mode with variance \(1/(2\beta)\) under a positive one. A subnormal shape, below the smallest normal double, is computed apart (see dmhn), and there \(\log F\) keeps its relative accuracy too; below a tilt \(z\) of about 52 (53 at the smallest shapes) pmhn is then 1 at every positive q.

When any of alpha, beta, gamma is a vector, the CDF is evaluated element-wise. The Fox-Wright \(\Psi\) normalizing constant is computed once for each position of the recycling cycle while that cycle is at most 256 long, and otherwise once for each run of consecutive elements that share the \((\alpha, \beta, \gamma)\) triple. So recycled parameters, and parameter vectors in which equal triples are adjacent, are much faster than triples that alternate along a long vector, and than calling pmhn inside an R loop.

The numerical methods, and the reasons for the ranges above, are described in Appendix A of vignette("theory", package = "mhn").

References

Sun, J., Kong, M., & Pal, S. (2023). The Modified-Half-Normal distribution: Properties and an efficient sampling scheme. Communications in Statistics - Theory and Methods, 52(5), 1591–1613.

See also

dmhn, qmhn, rmhn

Examples

# Basic evaluation
pmhn(c(0.5, 1, 1.5), alpha = 2, beta = 1, gamma = 1)
#> [1] 0.1129101 0.4338796 0.7614259

# Tail / log forms
pmhn(2, alpha = 2, beta = 1, gamma = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)
#> [1] 0.06369619
pmhn(2, alpha = 2, beta = 1, gamma = 1, log.p = TRUE)
#> [1] -0.06581527

# Special case: gamma = 0 reduces to sqrt-Gamma
all.equal(pmhn(1.5, alpha = 2, beta = 1, gamma = 0),
          pgamma(1.5^2, shape = 1, rate = 1))
#> [1] TRUE
